summary: Describes the tag URI scheme. Tag URIs are designed to be unique across space and time while remaining easy for humans to read and write. They have no authoritative resolution mechanism, and can be used simply as entity identifiers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A tag is a name for a thing that nobody is supposed to be able to take away from you. It is built from a domain name or email address plus the date you got that name, so two people who hold the same name on different days can never mint the same tag.

questions: how to create unique identifiers with tag uri
how to mint a tag uri
how do i mint a tag uri
subtitle: A way to mint names that nobody else can hand out, without asking anyone's permission first.

tldr.problem: People want names for their documents and objects that are unlikely to collide with anyone else's, can be created without registering anywhere, and are easy to read and type.
tldr.mechanism: A tag URI combines the domain name or email address of the person minting it with the date that name was assigned to them, followed by any string they choose, so two different holders of the same name can never mint the same tag.
tldr.outcome: Tags are identifiers only. They have no resolution mechanism, and the memo says that if resolution is wanted, a different URI scheme should be used instead.

today: RFC 4151 is an Informational memo published in October 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It records that IANA has registered the tag URI scheme as a permanent scheme.

sections.title: What A Tag Is For
sections.content:
A tag is a type of Uniform Resource Identifier designed to meet four requirements. Identifiers should be likely to be unique across space and time and come from a practically inexhaustible supply. They should be reasonably convenient for humans to create, read, type and remember. No central registration should be necessary, at least for holders of domain names or email addresses, and minting each new identifier should cost almost nothing. And the identifiers should be independent of any particular resolution scheme.

The memo gives the case of someone who wants to put identifiers on their documents. The user wants reasonable assurance of uniqueness, because global uniqueness stops identifiers from becoming unintentionally ambiguous. The identifiers should be tractable to mint, memorise and type into emails and forms. The user should not have to talk to anyone else to mint one. And the identifiers should avoid implying that an electronic resource exists at a location, when it does not.

Existing schemes meet some of these requirements but not all. UUIDs are hard for humans to read. OIDs and Digital Object Identifiers require entities to register as naming authorities even when they already hold a domain name. URLs, in particular http URLs, are often used as identifiers and satisfy most of the requirements, but they have drawbacks: someone may try to resolve a URL-as-identifier even though no resource is accessible there, and domain names change hands, so a new assignee cannot tell whether the previous holder already used a particular identifier. Lastly, many people, especially individuals, hold email addresses but not domain names, and it would be preferable to let them mint identifiers too.
sections.plainLanguage: People want names for their own files and objects that are hard to collide with, easy to make, and need no registration. A tag is designed to give exactly that, with no central authority involved.

sections.title: The Syntax Of A Tag URI
sections.content:
The general syntax of a tag URI is tag:, then a tagging entity, then a colon, then a specific string, optionally followed by a hash and a fragment. The tagging entity is made of an authority name and a date. The authority name is either a fully qualified domain name or an email address containing one, and it must be fully qualified so that there is no ambiguity. It is recommended that the domain name be in lower case, and alternative spellings of the same authority name are counted as distinct, so tags beginning tag:EXAMPLE.com,2000: are never equal to those beginning tag:example.com,2000:.

Authority names could in principle belong to any namespace whose names are assigned to a unique entity at a time, such as certain IP addresses, MAC addresses or telephone numbers. To keep the scheme simple the syntax is restricted to domain names and email addresses, but software that processes tags must not reject tags on the grounds that they fall outside this syntax, so that future standards efforts can add other forms.

The specific part is the name-space-specific string chosen by the minter, drawn from URI characters, and it may include query subcomponents as defined in the generic URI syntax. It is recommended that specific identifiers be human-friendly. A tag may optionally end in a fragment identifier, and tags should not be minted with percent-encoded parts, because humans find them hard to read, although the syntax does allow percent-encoded characters in the permitted character set.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag always has the same shape: the word tag, then your name, then a comma and a date, then a colon and whatever text you want to use. The part after the colon is yours to choose, and it can be as readable as you like.

sections.title: Rules For Minting Tags
sections.content:
Each tag carries a tagging entity, identified by an authority name and a date. The date is what makes the entity globally unique, exploiting the fact that domain names and email addresses are assigned to at most one entity at a time. That entity then ensures it mints unique identifiers itself.

The date names the day, in the Gregorian calendar and UTC, on which the authority name was assigned to the tagging entity at 00:00 UTC. It may be a past or present date, and it must be one of the YYYY, YYYY-MM and YYYY-MM-DD formats of the ISO 8601 standard. Tagging entities must ascertain the date accurately enough to avoid accidentally using a day on which the name was not in fact assigned, since many computers and mobile devices have poorly synchronised clocks. The date must be reckoned from UTC. The month and day default to 01, so 2001-07 means 2001-07-01 and 2000 means 2000-01-01, and every formulation names a moment rather than a period. Alternative spellings of the same date count as distinct, so tags beginning tag:example.com,2000: are never equal to those beginning tag:example.com,2000-01-01:.

An entity must not mint tags under an authority name that was assigned to a different entity at 00:00 UTC on the given date, and must not mint tags under a future date. An entity that acquires a name immediately after a period when it was unassigned may mint tags as if it had held the name throughout, but this practice has considerable potential for error and must not be used without substantial evidence that the name was unassigned; the authors know of no mechanism that counts as evidence other than daily polling of the whois registry.

Finally, a tagging entity mints specific identifiers that are unique within its own context, using any internal scheme built only from URI characters. It should keep records to achieve that uniqueness, and where many people share one authority name, as a corporation or a mailing list might, group decision-making should also be used. The outcome of such a decision could be to delegate control over parts of the namespace, so that the assignees of example.com could hand the prefixes tag:example.com,2004:fred: and tag:example.com,2004:bill: to two different people.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are about the date. Use the day you got your domain name or email address, count it from UTC, and never use a date when someone else held the name. Inside that space, you choose the rest of the tag and keep it unique yourself.

sections.title: Resolution And Equality
sections.content:
There is no authoritative resolution mechanism for tags. Unlike most other URIs, tags can only be used as identifiers and are not designed to support resolution. If authoritative resolution is a desired feature, a different URI scheme should be used.

Tags are simply strings of characters, and two tags are equal only if they are completely indistinguishable in their machine representations when using the same character encoding. In practice that means comparing the numeric codes of their characters in sequence. This criterion keeps tag-handling software simple, because it does not have to transform tags in any way to compare them.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot look up a tag to find a document. It is only a name, and two tags are the same only when every character matches exactly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Minting a tag is an operation internal to the tagging entity and has no external consequences. What happens when an improperly minted tag, from malice or error, is used in an application depends on the application and has to be considered in the design of any application that uses tags.

There is a significant possibility of minting errors, from people who fail to apply the rules governing dates or who use a shared organizational authority name without prior agreement across the organization. Tag-aware software may help catch these errors and warn against them, but software must not reject tags that do not conform to the syntax, so that the scheme can be extended later.

A malicious party could make it appear that the same domain name or email address was assigned to each of two or more entities. Tagging entities should use reputable assigning authorities and verify assignment wherever possible. They should also avoid the risk of clock-skew exploitation by using authority names that were held continuously from well before to well after 00:00 UTC on the chosen date, preferably by intervals in the order of days.
sections.plainLanguage: Making a tag does not affect anyone else, so the risk is in using one that was minted wrongly. Get the date right, agree with others if you share a name, and check who your name registrar says holds it.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The IANA has registered the tag URI scheme as specified in this document. The registered scheme name is tag and its status is permanent. The syntax is the one in Section 2. Percent-encoding is allowed in the specific and fragment components. The intended usage is as described in the introduction and in the section on resolution. Applications and protocols that use the scheme include any application that uses URIs as identifiers without requiring dereference, such as RDF, YAML and Atom. The interoperability considerations are recorded as none, and the security considerations are those in Section 3.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme is registered under the name tag with a permanent status. It is meant for formats such as RDF, YAML and Atom, which use URIs as labels rather than as addresses.

viz.caption: THE TAG URI SYNTAX IN ABNF (RFC 4151 SECTION 2.1)

data.title: tagURI
data.code:
tagURI = "tag:" taggingEntity ":" specific [ "#" fragment ]

taggingEntity = authorityName "," date
authorityName = DNSname / emailAddress
date = year ["-" month ["-" day]]
year = 4DIGIT
month = 2DIGIT
day = 2DIGIT
DNSname = DNScomp *( "."  DNScomp ) ; see RFC 1035
DNScomp = alphaNum [*(alphaNum /"-") alphaNum]
emailAddress = 1*(alphaNum /"-"/"."/"_") "@" DNSname
alphaNum = DIGIT / ALPHA
specific = *( pchar / "/" / "?" ) ; pchar from RFC 3986
fragment = *( pchar / "/" / "?" ) ; same as RFC 3986

viz.caption: WHY THE EXISTING SCHEMES FALL SHORT (RFC 4151 SECTION 1)

cells: Require entities to register as naming authorities, even when they already hold a domain name.
Someone may try to resolve one even though no resource is there, and a domain name can change hands.

items.title: Use your own name
items.text: Mint only under a fully qualified domain name or email address that is assigned to you.

items.title: Date it correctly
items.text: Use the day the authority name was assigned to you, reckoned from UTC, in YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD form.

items.title: Never use someone else's name
items.text: An entity must not mint tags under an authority name that was assigned to a different entity on that date.

items.title: No future dates
items.text: Tags dated in the future are not allowed.

items.title: Unassigned periods are risky
items.text: Minting as if the name were held while it was unassigned is allowed only with solid evidence.

items.title: Keep your part unique
items.text: Use record keeping, and group decisions where many people mint under one name.
